newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania campaign closes with fierce exchanges.
newsitem.headline: Romania campaign closes with fierce exchanges.

text.p: Romania's presidential election campaign closed in a blaze of acrimony with incumbent Ion Iliescu rejecting charges that his seven years in office had produced a society riven with poverty and corruption.
Iliescu, an ex-communist who came to power after the 1989 execution of dictator Nicolae Ceausescu, finished four points ahead of academic Emil Constantinescu in the opening round.
But the opposition forced the president's ruling party out of government in general elections and Constantinescu says his election on Sunday would end the communist legacy for good.

In the last of four lengthy television debates on Thursday evening, Constantinescu accused Iliescu of plunging the country into grinding poverty at the head of an administration uncommitted to reform and wallowing in corruption.
"Ours is a rich country with poor people. Wealth was concentrated in the hands of a political class surrounding you," Constantinescu said, his voice rarely changing in tone.
"You have become alienated from the people. Don't believe for a minute that your pre-arranged visits with body guards and limousines can be considered dialogue with the people."
Did the president, he asked, believe a family of four could live on monthly wages equal to $50 - common for many workers.
"I am aware of such things. I come from a modest family and have had a life with privations," Iliescu replied.
"I wanted a reform model to ensure economic integration and help for the needy. It is not for a lack of understanding that we have difficulties. Your approach is superficial."
In an aggressive final round campaign, the president warned farmers and workers that Constantinescu would restore pre-war landowners liable to reclaim their homes and shut factories.

He also suggested the bearded academic was prepared to betray national interests by offering special autonomy to 1.6 million ethnic Hungarians. Constantinescu rejected the allegations as a desperate bid to cling to power.

He wants to proceed with his Democratic Convention (CDR)'s programme to cut taxes, increase social benefits and kick-start the economy within 200 days and close the gap in living standards with ex-Communist states like Hungary and Poland.

The CDR will form the backbone of the new government, along with former Prime Minister Petre Roman's Social Democrats. Roman finished third in the opening round and has thrown his support in the run-off to Constantinescu.
Moral issues have figured prominently in the campaign.

Constantinescu, like many liberals, says ex-Communists "hijacked" the 1989 revolution to hold power. He also accused Iliescu of encouraging rampages through Bucharest by miners in the early 1990s to block reforms and leapfrog over rivals.
Iliescu replied that he acted in the national interest.

In the final debate, Iliescu said for the second time that he believed in and "feared" God -- an important matter in a country where 86 percent of the population adhere at least nominally to the Orthodox church.
"The ninth commandment says "Thou shalt not bear false witness.' Yet you lied with such ease in the campaign and allowed so much hatred to be spread," Constantinescu said.
"You do not fear God."
Iliescu said his campaign had faced untold smears, like suggestions of links to the former Soviet KGB security service.
"You have no moral authority to speak about such things," he said. "You must be more responsible if you aspire to the highest office in the country."
